meta_description: Personal website of Anton Lechuga - science, running, music, and references.
study_text: I have an interdisciplinary background in social science and computer science. I am interested in the influence of current AI on society (positive and negative), and in how AI can be used to benefit society and enable humans rather than replace them.
work_text: My professional career is currently focused on cloud deployment and DevOps. My interest here is to ensure secure, stable deployments that are EU-law compliant and tailored to the customers' wishes.
life_text: I focus on AI and data science, spanning the full pipeline from organising and modelling client data to analysing it for insights or building models based on it. I have researched the robustness and explainability of deep-learning-based models across various domains.
quote_text: Enjoy the little detours to the fullest. Because that's where you'll find things more important than what you want!
running_text: After some break, I am currently concentrating on getting back to regular running (> 80 km weekly) and getting the best out of my body. I want to top my PBs, which I all set over the past two years.
music_text: Music is my passion, and I'm into all kinds of rock, metal and electronic music. blog_description: Personal notes about ideas worth developing in my own words.
blog_post_why_title: Why I Am Starting a Blog in the Age of AI
blog_post_why_excerpt: I want a future in which human thought and agency still matter. This blog is my attempt to practise that: forming my own opinions, exploring unusual ideas, and giving questions my full attention.
blog_post_why_body_1: I am starting this blog because I want to explore a future in which human thought and agency remain relevant as AI becomes more capable. By agency, I mean our ability to form judgments, choose what matters to us, and act on those choices. This also raises a practical question for me: how can I preserve these abilities in my own use of AI? Writing gives me a way to work through that question. Three motivations are central to this blog.
blog_post_why_body_2: First, I want to develop opinions that I can justify. When an AI offers a well-formulated argument, it can be difficult to distinguish between a view I have examined myself and one I have simply become familiar with. I worry that I might begin to treat a suggested opinion as my own. Writing without AI requires me to formulate the argument, identify its assumptions, and decide whether I agree with it. I want to make time for that process, including the uncomfortable stages when my thoughts are still unclear.
blog_post_why_body_3: Research suggests that AI writing suggestions can influence our views. In a 2023 experiment, Maurice Jakesch and colleagues had people write about social media, some with an assistant configured to favour a particular view. The assistant influenced both their texts and their answers in a subsequent attitude survey. That shows an immediate opinion shift after a writing task with a deliberately opinionated model. It does not establish that the shift lasts or that every use of AI has this effect. It makes me want to try forming my own view before asking for suggestions.
blog_post_why_body_4: Second, I want to explore ideas beyond established ways of thinking. Language models are impressive at bringing together existing knowledge and combining it into useful, sometimes surprising solutions. However, I still consider people more likely to make certain radical departures, including questioning the assumptions behind a problem or changing the question itself. This is my intuition, rather than an established difference between human and machine creativity. The blog gives me a place to examine it by exploring topics outside the mainstream and developing arguments whose conclusions are not obvious from the start. I also enjoy following an unusual idea to see where it leads, while remaining willing to reject it if the argument does not hold.
blog_post_why_body_5: An experiment by Anil Doshi and Oliver Hauser makes me wonder about the directions we might miss. Access to AI ideas helped people write very short stories judged more creative, especially those who scored lower on a creativity test. Yet the stories were more similar to one another than those written without AI ideas. This does not establish who can produce the most radical ideas. But if we increasingly start from similar suggestions, which possible directions might we never explore?
blog_post_why_body_6: Third, I want to give difficult topics sustained attention. A summary can make a subject easier to approach, but reading one does not necessarily mean that I have understood the underlying argument. If I repeatedly delegate the reading, comparison, and evaluation to AI, I may also skip the work through which I would develop that understanding. This blog gives me a reason to read sources myself, examine disagreements, and follow a question beyond its first plausible answer. Choosing where to direct my attention is part of the agency I want to preserve.
blog_post_why_body_7: Related research looks at how much critical thinking we do when using AI. In a 2025 survey of 319 knowledge workers, Hao-Ping Lee and colleagues found that greater confidence in AI handling a particular task was associated with a lower likelihood of reporting critical thinking during that task. This was a one-off survey based on self-reports; it did not measure attention or establish cause and effect. For me, it prompts a question about my own habits: which parts of understanding am I still doing myself?
blog_post_why_body_8: Together, these motivations give the blog a practical purpose: to develop my own judgments, explore unfamiliar ideas, and study questions in enough depth to understand them. I expect my views to change through that process. For this post, I began by speaking through my motivations; AI helped with research, drafting, and the English and German wording. Writing without that help is something I want to make time for as this blog develops.
